title: DICE: Domain-attack Invariant Causal Learning for Improved Data Privacy Protection and Adversarial Robustness

problem.claim: Adversarial attacks can expose model vulnerability or inject malicious noise to protect private data, while adversarial training can defend against both attacks.

gap.claim: Adversarial training has poor robustness generalization, and attack and defense methods can rely on spurious rather than causal relations.

contributions.claim: The paper develops the Domain-attack Invariant Causal Model (DICM) to analyze attack-induced domain shifts and their effects on deep neural networks.
The paper proposes a coherent causal invariant principle to guide algorithm design toward human-like causal relations.
The paper proposes Domain-attack Invariant Causal Learning (DICE).

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report experimental results on two attacks and one defense task as verifying DICE's effectiveness.

narrative_sequence.summary: Attacks create domain shifts or privacy concerns, and adversarial training can defend against them.
Adversarial training generalizes poorly, while attacks and defenses may exploit spurious relations rather than causal relations.
The paper analyzes latent factors, observed data, and attack-induced domain shifts before developing DICM.
DICM motivates a causal invariant principle and the DICE algorithm.
The authors report experiments covering two attacks and one defense task.

source_observation.claim: Spurious input-output relations can be exploited by attacks and defenses and can reduce robustness under domain shift.

interpretation.claim: Robustness-oriented methods should distinguish stable causal relations from correlations that change across attack-induced domains.

application.claim: When designing attack or defense methods, analyze latent factors and domain shifts before selecting the learning objective.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that causal modeling alone resolves all attack or defense limitations.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, attack implementations, defense configuration, evaluation metrics, baselines, or quantitative results.
The abstract does not provide implementation details, computational requirements, or reproducibility information.
